herastrau-park.name: King Michael I (Herăstrău) Park: Alley of Personalities, Japanese Garden & south lakeshore
herastrau-park.blurb: Bucharest's biggest park: an alley of 30 stone busts of world writers and composers, a Japanese garden and the tip of Lake Herăstrău.

footprint.note: ~400 m E-W x 410 m N-S in the south-west of the park between Piața Charles de Gaulle entrance (SE) and the Arc/Village Museum edge (W), up to the southern tip of the lake (N, shore at ~44.4713,26.0803). Park total 187 ha incl. 74 ha lake.

structures.name: Alley of busts (Aleea Personalităților / Aleea Michael Jackson area)
structures.note: Asphalt alleys lined by ~30 stone/marble busts on plinths (OSM tourism=artwork with artist names): Goethe, Shakespeare, Victor Hugo, Mark Twain, Leonardo da Vinci, Beethoven, Brâncuși, Eminescu, Caragiale, Tolstoy, Chekhov, Balzac, Petőfi, Ady Endre, Bartók, Botev, Levski, Glinka, Naim Frashëri, Grigore Vieru, Nicolae Grigorescu, Theodor Aman...

items: Nimfa adormită (Sleeping Nymph), marble, Filip Marin (node/1342884103)

Fata babei și fata moșului (Constantin Foamete)

structures.name: Michael Jackson memorial plaque
structures.note: Marble plaque by a tree: "MICHAEL J. JACKSON - HIS MUSIC WILL LIVE FOREVER"; fans leave flowers/candles; his 1 Oct 1992 Bucharest concert was filmed for the HBO special "Live in Bucharest: The Dangerous Tour" (verify before using as a plaque fact)

structures.name: Grădina Japoneză
structures.note: Small ponds with arched red/wood bridge, stone lanterns, Japanese cherries (sakura, bloom early-mid April), maples, raked gravel; open 07:00-22:00 (OSM)

structures.name: Lake Herăstrău south tip
structures.note: Concrete/stone embankment with railings, ducks and swans, pedal boats and the lake tour boats (vaporașe) from the Debarcader pier further north

vegetation.summary: Mature parkland: lindens, horse chestnuts, oaks, plane trees, poplars and willows on the shore; ornamental cherries and Japanese maples in the Japanese Garden; rose beds. Few trees mapped in OSM here - use dense deciduous canopy over alleys.

herastrau-park.lighting: Park lamps along alleys; lake reflects the city; Japanese garden dark at night.
herastrau-park.backdrop: Lake with tree-lined far shore and high-rise towers of Floreasca/Barbu Văcărescu beyond; Charles de Gaulle square with the General's bronze statue (SE).

crowd.typical: Joggers, cyclists, rollerbladers, families with strollers, retirees on benches, couples, picnickers, dog walkers; weekends very busy; Park was the most-searched park by foreign tourists (Visit Bucharest 2022).

ambient_sounds: boat motor of the lake tour

plaques.title: 187 hectares
plaques.text: The park covers about 187 ha, of which 74 ha is Lake Herăstrău.

plaques.title: From marsh to park
plaques.text: The marshes were drained in 1930-1935 and the park opened in 1936 as the National Park.

plaques.title: Many names
plaques.text: It was named Carol II Park, then I. V. Stalin Park (with a Stalin statue), Herăstrău in 1956 and King Michael I Park in 2017.

plaques.title: Why "Herăstrău"
plaques.text: "Herăstrău" comes from "ferăstrău" (saw): water-powered sawmills once stood on the Colentina river.

plaques.title: Mammoths
plaques.text: Mammoth bones and Neanderthal-era flint tools were found in the Herăstrău sand quarry.

interaction.true_to_place: The busts alley and the Japanese garden are the signature features of this corner of the park.

village-museum.name: Dimitrie Gusti National Village Museum
village-museum.blurb: A whole Romanian village of real wooden houses, churches and mills moved to the shore of Lake Herăstrău in 1936.

footprint.note: ~360 m E-W x 420 m N-S: the southern half of the museum from the main entrance on Șos. Kiseleff 28-30 (Bd. Regele Mihai I) towards the lake, covering the Oltenia/Muntenia/Transylvania/Maramureș sectors around the entrance. Fenced museum (ticketed). The museum overall is 778 x 264 m (OSM way/29701978, 10 ha).

structures.name: Main entrance & ticket office (Kiseleff 28-30)
structures.note: Wooden gate structure with shingled roof in traditional carved style; ticket booth, souvenir shop (Galeria de Artă Țărănească), toilets; OSM entrance=main

structures.name: Wooden church from Dragomirești, Maramureș (1718-1722)
structures.osm: way/277782593 (building=church, material=wood, 15.8 x 6.6 m, long axis ~87 deg E-W; graveyard crosses OSM nodes 13004324741.. just south) - identified as Dragomirești by being the only wooden church in this sector; verify against refs
structures.note: Museum centrepiece and logo: log church on a low river-stone plinth; lower skirt roof sheltering an open porch gallery with a plank balustrade, then a very steep main roof, from which rises a square shingle-clad tower with a projecting belfry gallery (small eave) and a tall needle spire with an orb and wrought-iron triple cross (total >35 m per press; unverified); everything clad in small wooden shingles (șiță); a tall spruce stands next to it; moved here in 1936 (photo: Biserica de lemn din Dragomirești, Maramureș.jpg)

structures.name: Gospodăria din Ieud, Maramureș
structures.note: Maramureș household with the iconic carved monumental wooden gate (poartă maramureșeană) with a small shingled roof, rope-twist motifs

structures.name: Peasant households (selection in footprint, OSM-named)
items: Gospodărie din Goicea Mică, Dolj (way/277782402, semi-buried dwelling)
Gospodărie din Măldărești, Vâlcea (way/277782435, fortified culă-type house)
Teasc de stors ceara, Sebeșu de Jos (way/525462874)
structures.materials: log walls (oak/fir, often whitewashed clay-plastered #EDE7DA in the south), steep shingle (șiță) or reed/straw roofs (#8C7B5E), carved verandas (prispă) with turned posts, blue-painted window frames in some Oltenia houses (#4A6C8C), wattle fences, wooden wells with sweep (cumpănă)

structures.name: Palatul Elisabeta (backdrop, inaccessible)
structures.note: Royal family residence enclave inside the museum area; white villa glimpsed behind trees; access=no

ground.surface: compacted earth/gravel paths and some asphalt/stone footways (OSM footway), grass everywhere

vegetation.summary: Old parkland: oaks, lindens, walnuts, fruit trees (plums, apples) in households, willows towards the lake, lilac and hollyhocks by houses; few trees mapped in OSM (1) - model as dense deciduous canopy along alleys with sunny clearings around houses.

street_furniture: information panels (bilingual RO/EN) for each household
14 OSM artworks (busts of EU founders lie just outside to the east)
village-museum.lighting: Daytime venue (OSM opening_hours Mo 09-17, Tu-Su 09-19); minimal path lamps. Model dusk at closing.
village-museum.backdrop: Lake Herăstrău glimpses to the north/east, Bd. Regele Mihai I (Kiseleff) traffic beyond the fence to the west, Ministry of Culture building at the entrance.

crowd.typical: Families, school groups, foreign tourists (68% foreign in 2017), artisans at weekend fairs (pottery, carved spoons, painted eggs at Easter), costumed folk dancers at festivals.

ambient_sounds: toaca (wooden semantron) beating at the church on feast days

plaques.title: Opened 1936
plaques.text: Opened on 10 May 1936 by sociologist Dimitrie Gusti in the presence of King Carol II; the 4th open-air museum in Europe.

plaques.title: A whole country
plaques.text: Over 100,000 m² with 123 authentic peasant households, 363 monuments and over 50,000 objects from all regions of Romania.

plaques.title: 56 railway wagons
plaques.text: The first buildings were dismantled in their villages and brought to Bucharest in 56 railway wagons.

plaques.title: Dragomirești church
plaques.text: The wooden church from Dragomirești (Maramureș), built 1718-1722, is the museum's centrepiece and logo.

plaques.title: The 2002 fire
plaques.text: A fire on 20 February 2002 destroyed 19 structures, including houses from Voitinel, Straja and Fundu Moldovei.

plaques.title: Visitors
plaques.text: In 2017 the museum had about 800,000 visitors, 68% of them foreigners.

interaction.title: Draw water from the well
interaction.desc: Use a well sweep (cumpănă) to lift a bucket, then walk the alley to the Dragomirești church and strike the toaca (wooden semantron) rhythm on feast days; collect a stamp from 5 regional households (Maramureș, Transylvania, Oltenia, Muntenia, Moldova) for the "village passport".
interaction.true_to_place: Wells with sweeps, toaca and region-grouped households are exactly what the museum shows.

photo_angle.note: From the lawn ~40 m south-west of the wooden church (OSM way/277782593 at 44.47145,26.07900) looking NE up at the west tower spire with the graveyard crosses in the foreground.

seasonal_time_of_day: Summer: festivals, folk dances, long evenings.
Autumn: Târgul Meșterilor Populari craft fairs, falling leaves on shingle roofs.
Winter: snow on steep roofs - most photogenic; Christmas carol (colinde) events.

culture.note: "Bună ziua" (good day) is the safe greeting with strangers; "Salut"/"Hey" among young people. Use "dumneavoastră" (formal you) with older people; elderly men may still say "Sărut mâna" (I kiss your hand) to women as an old-fashioned courtesy. Thank you = "Mulțumesc" or the very common French loan "Mersi".
Bună dimineața (morning), Bună ziua (day), Bună seara (evening); Noapte bună only when parting at night. Pick by the scene clock.

Romanian is a Romance language; young educated people usually speak good English, older educated people often French/Italian/Spanish. Italians/Spanish tourists often half-understand Romanian signs. So bubbles: Romanian for locals with English translation; tourists speak their own language.

Foreign visitors to Bucharest searching online in 2024 came mostly from UK, US, Germany, Bulgaria, Italy, Greece, Israel, Netherlands and France; British searched for Therme, Americans for "Wednesday" filming locations and Romanian food, Bulgarians for Christmas markets/concerts. Use these origins for tourist personas.
Never assume a car will stop at a crosswalk; drivers can be inconsiderate. Locals joke and grumble about traffic, honking, sidewalk parking and buses; keep it good-humoured, never aggressive.

Typical words: mici/mititei (grilled minced-meat rolls), ciorbă de burtă (tripe soup), sarmale (cabbage rolls), papanași (doughnuts with sour cream and jam), covrigi (pretzels sold from street windows). Caru' cu Bere, Berăria H and Hanu' lui Manuc were the most-searched restaurants by foreign tourists in 2024.

Orthodox churches (Stavropoleos, Patriarchal/National Cathedral): people cross themselves when passing, speak quietly, women often cover their heads, shoulders/knees covered; avoid flash and ask before photographing services. Nuns/priests are greeted with "Bună ziua" or "Doamne-ajută" (God help); do not script jokes about clergy.
culture.source: general Orthodox etiquette (no single source fetched from this environment - verify with church staff signage)

culture.note: Romanians are hospitable and insist when offering something ("no" is often treated as politeness and the offer repeated) - vendors/elders can repeat an offer once before accepting a refusal. Respect for the elderly is valued; older men may kiss a lady's hand; handshakes are standard.

Vlad the Impaler is seen by many Romanians as a national hero; some are offended when he is equated with Count Dracula - so locals in bubbles push back ("Vlad Țepeș was one of ours, not a vampire!"). Opinions on Ceaușescu vary; some older people speak of him positively - an elder persona may be nostalgic, others critical; never caricature either.
Avoid lines implying Romanian is Slavic or that Romania was part of the USSR; never confuse Romanians with Roma people.
Unsolicited offers of help/taxis near tourist areas can be scams; locals recommend Bolt/Uber. A vendor/tout persona may push magnets or taxis politely; the player can just walk away.

Communism and Ceaușescu are top tourist interests ("Communism and communist buildings remain at the top of searches"). Locals talk about it with dark irony (e.g. calling the Memorial of Rebirth "the impaled potato"), but lines must stay factual and avoid mocking victims of 1989 (around 1,500 died).

Do not use ethnic jokes (in particular about Roma people) or Dracula/vampire clichés aimed at locals; Dracula appears only as souvenir-vendor patter and as a historical fact (Vlad III built the Old Princely Court).

1 March: mărțișor (red-and-white string trinkets) sold everywhere and given to women; December: "Crăciun fericit!" and the Christmas market in Piața Constituției; winter: "Ce ger!" (what frost); summer heatwaves: "caniculă" (summers often exceed 30 °C).
